sentences.t: ANMI's International Capital Market Convention - the broking industry's own gathering, at its sixteenth edition this year - is where SEBI's chairman, Tuhin Kanta Pandey, used the stage to read out what amounts to a work order for the market's next rebuild.
Not a vision speech about grand themes: it runs four pillars - simpler rules, deeper markets, responsible technology, wider access - across about a dozen items.
This article takes the four that would change the market's structure most.
The audience matters for reading the speech.
Brokers are the industry that carries the compliance load, operates the lending desks and will run - or resist - every one of these changes.
A chairman who tells this room that compliance will be graded by scale, client exposure and technology reliance, and that short-selling rules are under review, is not testing slogans.
He is telling the people who will have to build it.
Here is what is on the list, what each item really does, and what has to happen next for any of it to be real.
India's corporate-bond market is big and strangely invisible.
About Rs 61 lakh crore is outstanding - the chairman's own figure - and almost none of it trades where a saver can see it.
The market runs institution to institution, over the phone and through dealers, in ticket sizes built for institutions.

A fixed deposit is simple but locks you in; equity is liquid but volatile; the bond in between, which should be the natural third asset, has let retail into eligible privately placed issues at Rs 10,000 since July 2024 - but barely lets it out, because secondary trading is thin and the exit is where the cost sits.
The chairman's answer has a name: Demat 2.0.
In the 1990s, dematerialisation took share certificates out of paper and put them in electronic accounts, and equity trading exploded.
Demat 2.0 is the same idea for bonds - and it is not a proposal.

SEBI launched the pilot on 10 September: three issuers - REC, L&T and IIFL - have raised Rs 1,025 crore in tokenised corporate bonds, settled atomically against the RBI's wholesale CBDC and held in ordinary demat accounts.
First-phase issuance was still running at the 10 September launch.

The speech's news is what comes next: phase two, in which these bonds start trading in the secondary market; the launch release names the venue - the existing RFQ platforms - with retail access promised in a later phase.
To see what is actually being fixed, walk one transaction through both worlds.
Today: you want to lend Rs 10 lakh to a solid company for three years.
You can - since July 2024, privately placed bonds come in Rs 10,000 denominations and online bond platforms will sell you one.
What you cannot easily do is sell it again: secondary trading is thin, quotes are wide, and the exit, not the entry, is the real wall between households and bonds.

In the end state the chairman is pointing to: that company's bond exists as a token in your demat account, it trades on the RFQ platform, and settlement - the part that in the conventional market takes days - lands the same day, because the bond and the money move together on the RBI's CBDC rail.
Two dependencies decide whether this is real.
First, market-makers - the speech separately lists a bond market-making framework, and it is the unglamorous half of the idea, because a token nobody quotes is a fixed deposit with extra steps.
Second, the small print on credit risk: a retail-tradable bond market also makes it easier to sell weak paper to the least protected buyer.
How the framework grades issuers will matter as much as the token itself.
Betting against a stock in India is hard, expensive and rare.

The mechanism for it - securities lending and borrowing, SLB, the pipe through which you borrow shares to sell them short - exists but stays thin, while futures and options carry most of the scepticism.
The chairman said the short-selling framework and SLB are under review.
Why a regulator would want stronger shorts is not cynicism; it is price discovery.
A market where doubt is expensive is a market where bad stories last longer.
When sceptics cannot borrow stock cheaply, the first honest signal of trouble arrives late and all at once.
A working SLB market lets the bear case get priced gradually instead of detonating.
Watch for the review's shape: borrow costs, eligible-stock lists, and whether large shareholders are nudged to lend idle stock.
If the review ends in a consultation paper with real relaxations, crowded long trades get a new counterweight.
If it ends in a study, nothing changes.
Ask a two-branch brokerage what compliance costs and you get a number that decides whether the firm survives; ask a bank-owned giant and you get a department.

The chairman told the room - the room that pays these bills - that SEBI is exploring graded compliance: obligations scaled to an intermediary's scale, client exposure and reliance on technology - the chairman's three factors.
This is the item with the most immediate constituency and the least public glamour.
Its second-order effect is competition: a compliance load that is flat in size is a moat for the big and a wall for the small.

Grading it changes how many brokers can exist, which changes what distribution costs - and in a country where the same firms distribute mutual funds, bonds and insurance, that cost eventually reaches every saver's statement.
The last item is further along than it looks.

Market intermediaries already run AI - in surveillance, in client onboarding, in robo-advice, in order routing - and the regulator's rulebook is not a blank page: SEBI put out a consultation paper on the responsible use of AI and ML in June 2025.

The chairman's news is that the final guidelines are now being finalised - tiered by risk, with clear accountability, data controls and kill switches, aligned with IOSCO, the global standard-setter's toolkit - plus a newer, earlier-stage idea: an AI sandbox the speech says SEBI is exploring, where new tools can be tested safely.
The detail to hold is "kill switches".

A guideline that requires a market AI to be stoppable is a guideline written by someone who has read the failure modes: models do not get tired or conflicted; they get wrong, at scale, at machine speed.

Tiering matters for the same reason - a chatbot answering account questions and a model routing institutional orders are not the same risk, and a flat rule would either strangle the first or under-police the second.
A SEBI idea travels a known road: signal, consultation paper, board approval, circular.

The four items are not at the same station - the bond pilot is already running and the AI guidelines are past consultation - which is why the honest reading of this speech is not "reform is coming" but "reform is at different stations, and each station has an observable marker".
The checklist, item by item:

Demat 2.0 moves to phase two if tokenised bonds start trading on the RFQ platforms, with the market-making framework the speech separately lists arriving alongside - and if the retail-access phase in the launch release follows.
It stalls if issuance stops at three issuers and Rs 1,025 crore.
The short-selling review is real if it ends in a published consultation paper on borrow costs and eligible stock - and a slogan if it ends in a committee that never surfaces.
Graded compliance is real if the next broker-regulation consultation actually sorts obligations by scale, client exposure and technology reliance.
The AI framework is real if the final guidelines land with the promised tiering and kill switches - and the sandbox moves from "exploring" to a dated pilot.

The markers to watch are public and dated: consultation papers, board-outcome press releases and circulars on SEBI's website - not board agenda papers, which SEBI has published only after decisions since its 2008 transparency rules.
If none of the four produces a document over the next two board cycles, the correct reading of the ANMI speech is that it was a speech.

If even two produce them, the correct reading is that the market's plumbing is about to be rebuilt - and the winners are the saver who gets a third asset, the small broker who gets to keep existing, and the sceptic who finally gets to borrow.
A speech that tells you where each item stands - and which document comes next - is rare.
This one did.
The consultation papers, board outcomes and circulars are where to grade it.
